reason: The passage describes the opposite dynamic: the people and their wives cry out (צַעֲקַת הָעָ֛ם) about their suffering and oppression (lack of grain, mortgaged fields, enslaved children). In response, Nehemiah becomes angry (וַיִּחַר לִ֖י מְאֹ֑ד) at hearing their complaint. He then confronts the rulers and officials (הַחֹרִ֣ים וְאֶת־ הַסְּגָנִ֔ים), rebuking them for exacting from their brothers (מַשָּׁ֥א אִישׁ־ בְּאָחִ֖יו). Nehemiah, as a leader, criticizes other leaders for their oppression of the people—he does not complain about the people themselves. The leadership's conduct toward the people is the object of complaint, not the people's behavior.
